## 9. Algorithms

The theory is entirely constructive, and each theorem corresponds to a small exact algorithm.

**Algorithm A (Fermat–Weber set of a sample on a line).** Sort the sample $x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(n)}$ in $O(n\log n)$ (or $O(n)$ by selection). Return $[x_{(k+1)}, x_{(k+1)}]$ if $n = 2k+1$, and $[x_{(k)}, x_{(k+1)}]$ if $n = 2k$. Correctness: Corollary 3.6 and Theorem 4.1. The optimal cost is $\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{(n+1-i)} - x_{(i)}\bigr)$ over $i\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor$, i.e. the sum of nested spreads.

**Algorithm B (balance test).** Given $S$ and $m$, compute $\#\{x\le m\}$, $\#\{x<m\}$ in one pass, $O(n)$; report balanced iff $n - \#\{x\le m\} \le \#\{x\le m\}$ and $\#\{x<m\} \le n - \#\{x<m\}$. By Theorem 3.9 this is an exact optimality certificate — no cost evaluation required.

**Algorithm C (stability radius of the centre).** Given a sample with one designated free coordinate, the set of values of that coordinate leaving the reported centre unchanged is, by Theorem 5.5, a half-line when the centre is at an endpoint of the segment spanned by the fixed data, and a singleton otherwise. For the measured $16\times$ data (fixed $\{224,256\}$) it is $(-\infty, 224]$, so the stability radius *downwards* is infinite and *upwards* is $0^+$.

**Algorithm D (ray/dilation diagnostics).** For paired measurements $(c_1,y_1)$, $(c_2,y_2)$, compute the determinant $c_1y_2 - y_1c_2$; zero certifies a proportional law and its slope, nonzero quantifies the departure by the origin-triangle area $|{\det}|/2$. For a doubling pair, the defect $2y_1 - y_2$ is the scalar measuring failure of dilation equivariance.

---

## 10. Discussion

### 10.1 What the geometry bought

Three informal claims were in circulation, and the geometry adjudicated all three.

*"The median is the robust quantity."* Made precise: the median of three is a metric projection onto the segment spanned by the other two, hence firmly nonexpansive with an unbounded stability half-line at each endpoint (Theorems 5.3–5.5). The mean, by contrast, is surjective in the free coordinate (Proposition 5.10). The claim is true, and quantitatively so.

*"Only a third seed $\ge 256$ would move the centre."* **False** (Proposition 5.8): the threshold is $224$, the near endpoint, as $\operatorname{med}(256,224,240) = 240$ shows. Intuition placed the boundary at the wrong end of the segment.

*"The $16\times$ spread is $\sim 50\%$ wider."* Exactly right, and exactly $3/2$ (Theorem 6.8), with the widening carried wholly by the low coordinate (Theorem 6.9).

### 10.2 Point predictions versus structural predictions

The round separates two kinds of claim. Four *point* predictions about a single seed's knee were all refuted. One *structural* prediction — about the centre of the distribution — held. The geometry explains why this asymmetry is not luck. A single seed's knee is determined by where a noisy quality curve crosses a bar between grid points; the reported measurement crossed with a margin of $+0.0012$, so the true threshold lies near $150$–$160$ and the grid reports $160$. Nothing protects that number. The median, by contrast, is the image of a firmly nonexpansive projection, and the projection's fibre over the reported value is an entire half-line: it is insensitive to arbitrarily large excursions in the protected direction.

The practical lesson generalises well beyond this dataset. When a per-run measurement is grid-quantised and noisy, do not pre-register the run's value; pre-register a functional of the distribution whose stability you can bound in advance. The stability bound *is* the prediction's content.

### 10.3 Limits and honesty

Several caveats are structural rather than rhetorical.

* The $7/8$ law rests on two contexts and six measurements. Two points determine a ray, so the "confirmation" in Theorem 6.4 is one independent test, not many. A third context would be the first genuine multiplicity.
* The low-tail ratio $5/8$ rests on a single measurement. Theorem 6.6's defect $P/8$ is therefore an exactly proved statement about one measured pair, not a verified law.
* The most recent knee reading was razor thin ($+0.0012$ margin against a binomial standard error of about $0.11\%$ in accuracy), so $160$ should be read as "the grid point above a threshold near $150$–$160$", not as an exact value.
* Theorem 8.2 shows the pending fourth measurement cannot refute the centre. This is a limitation on what the next experiment can tell us, and the correct response is to read that experiment as a test of the low tail, per Section 8.

### 10.4 Beyond the line

Two directions in which the results are already stated more generally than the data requires are worth flagging. Theorem 2.3 lives in an arbitrary metric space, and Corollary 2.5 shows that collinear data in a normed space have their geometric median *in the ambient space* at the middle point — the minimiser does not move off the line. Theorem 3.3 lives in an arbitrary linearly ordered abelian group, so the sufficiency half of the characterisation applies verbatim to integer, rational, or lexicographic data. Only the necessity half (Theorem 3.8) uses the reals, and even then only through the existence of a nearest datum on each side — so it holds in any linear order with the finite-sample structure used, i.e. essentially unchanged for integer grids, which is the case relevant to grid-quantised measurements.

---

## 11. Future directions

### C1. The fourth-value dichotomy: a new measurement can widen the optimal set but never move it

**Conjecture.** For the pending $16\times$ fourth value $x$, the Fermat–Weber optimum of $\{160,224,256,x\}$ is the segment with endpoints $\min(x,224)\vee 160$ and $\max(x,224)\wedge 256$, whose *endpoint at $224$ is pinned for every $x$*, while the optimal cost is $96 + |224-x|$. Consequently no fourth value can refute the $7/8$ centre in the variational sense; it can only destroy uniqueness, and it does so unless $x = 224$ exactly.

**Status.** The pinning, the cost law, both regime descriptions, and the uniqueness knife edge are established above (Theorems 8.1–8.5). What remains conjectural is the *empirical* half: that the measured fourth value lands in $[160,256]$, so that the segment description applies with both endpoints interior.

**Key insight.** With an even sample the Fermat–Weber minimiser is not a point but the middle segment, so "the median" of a four-measurement experiment is a *set*, and the correct falsifiable statement concerns the position of that set's endpoints, not a number.

**Why now.** The next planned experiment is exactly a fourth seed at $\mathrm{ctx}=2048$; stating the prediction as a segment before the run makes the outcome decidable in advance.

### C2. The low-tail ray defect grows linearly in the context

**Conjecture.** Writing $L(\mathrm{ctx})$ for the smallest three-measurement knee at context $\mathrm{ctx}$, the plane points $(\mathrm{ctx}, L(\mathrm{ctx}))$ are *not* collinear with the origin, and the defect of the doubling dilation, $2L(\mathrm{ctx}) - L(2\,\mathrm{ctx})$, equals $P(2\,\mathrm{ctx})/8$ where $P = d\cdot\mathrm{ctx}/32$. The measured pair gives $2\cdot 96 - 160 = 32 = 256/8$.

**Status.** The single measured instance is exact (Theorem 6.6); the law itself is open. It needs a third context, $\mathrm{ctx}=4096$, with predicted low tail $2\cdot 160 - 512/8 = 256$, i.e. ratio $1/2$.

**Key insight.** The top edge and the median are dilation-equivariant while the low tail is not, so the entire context dependence of the knee *distribution* is concentrated in one scalar defect, measurable with a single extra run.

**Why now.** The $4096$ cell is one doubling away, and the prediction ratio $1/2$ is far from the alternative $5/8$ that would hold if the low tail were also equivariant; one run separates them.

### C3. Median stability as a firm-nonexpansiveness phenomenon, with a sharp constant

**Conjecture.** For any statistic $S:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ that is (i) symmetric, (ii) translation equivariant, (iii) monotone, and (iv) firmly nonexpansive in each coordinate with the others fixed, the stability set of a reported value — the set of values of a designated free coordinate leaving $S$ unchanged — is a closed interval, unbounded precisely when the reported value is an endpoint of the range of $S$ in that coordinate. The median satisfies all four hypotheses with sharp constant $1$; the mean fails (iv) in the required uniform sense and has singleton stability sets.

**Why it matters.** This would identify exactly which robust statistics inherit the half-line stability that made the $7/8$ law survivable, and would give a design criterion for choosing the reported functional in noisy threshold-search experiments.

### Further cells

Additional measurable directions: a fourth seed at $\mathrm{ctx}=1024$ to refine $\{96,112,128\}$ (low information value, since the median there is already pinned by the same projection argument); a depth-$8$ corner at short context to test whether the constant $7/8$ is depth-independent or specific to $d=4$; and a compression-floor check at depth $8$.

---

## 12. Conclusion

A distribution of noisy measurements was summarised by its median, and four point predictions about a single measurement failed while the structural claim about that median held. We have shown that this outcome is a theorem, not a coincidence.

The median on a line is the Fermat–Weber point: the minimiser of total distance. We characterised those minimisers completely — a point is optimal exactly when it is balanced — with sufficiency in any linearly ordered abelian group and a finitary necessity proof over the reals, and we showed the optimal set is always an interval, a point in odd size and a segment in even size. Holding two measurements fixed, the median of three is the nearest-point projection onto the segment they span: monotone, firmly nonexpansive, with half-line fibres at the endpoints. That is the mechanism of robustness, and it is quantitative: the measured excursion of $64$ units below the segment was absorbed exactly, and any excursion whatsoever in that direction would have been.

Across contexts, the picture is two rays and a defect. The upper edge and the median are exactly proportional to the context, with slopes $1/8$ and $7/64 = \tfrac78\cdot\tfrac18$; the low tail is not proportional at all, and the failure of dilation equivariance is the single scalar $P/8$. The spread grows by exactly $3/2$ per doubling, entirely through the low coordinate. Both normalised measurements lie on a maximal flat face of a non-convex level set of the median map, which is why they can agree at the centre while disagreeing everywhere else.

Finally, the geometry issues a prediction about the pending fourth measurement that cannot fail: the $7/8$ centre stays optimal whatever the new value is, the optimal cost is exactly $96 + |224 - x|$, and the optimum becomes a segment with one endpoint pinned at the centre. The right reading is that the next experiment is not a test of the centre but of the low tail — and stating that in advance, in the correct variational language, is the whole benefit of doing the geometry.
demo:
"""
Numerical demonstration of the geometry of a knee distribution.

This script is fully self-contained (standard library only, exact rational
arithmetic where it matters) and verifies, numerically, every quantitative
claim of the accompanying article and paper:

  1. Fermat-Weber cost on a line, its minimiser set, and the balance
     characterisation of optimality (any sample size, either parity).
  2. The measured three-value knee distributions at two context lengths, their
     geometric medians, and the 7/8 law  median = (7/8) * (d*ctx/32).
  3. The median of three as a nearest-point projection (clamp): monotonicity,
     nonexpansiveness, firm nonexpansiveness, fibre structure, range;
     the refutation of the informal claim "only values >= 256 move the centre".
  4. Scaling geometry: rays through the origin, the doubling dilation, the
     low-tail defect P/8, and the exact 3/2 spread ratio.
  5. The median level set in R^3: a maximal flat edge, the segment joining the
     two normalised measurements, and non-convexity of the level set.
  6. The pre-registered prediction for a pending fourth measurement: the centre
     224 stays optimal for every fourth value, the cost law 96 + |224 - x|,
     the two regimes, and the uniqueness knife edge.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Num = Fraction


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Fermat-Weber cost, minimiser set, and the balance certificate
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def fw_cost(sample: Sequence[Num], t: Num) -> Num:
    """Total distance from the candidate centre `t` to every sample point."""
    return sum((abs(t - x) for x in sample), Fraction(0))


def is_balanced(sample: Sequence[Num], m: Num) -> bool:
    """`m` is balanced: neither open side of `m` holds more than half the sample."""
    n_le = sum(1 for x in sample if x <= m)
    n_lt = sum(1 for x in sample if x < m)
    n = len(sample)
    return (n - n_le) <= n_le and n_lt <= (n - n_lt)


def fermat_weber_set(sample: Sequence[Num]) -> Tuple[Num, Num]:
    """Endpoints of the interval of minimisers of the total distance.

    Odd size 2k+1: the singleton [x_(k+1), x_(k+1)].
    Even size 2k : the middle segment [x_(k), x_(k+1)].
    """
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    if n % 2 == 1:
        mid = xs[n // 2]
        return (mid, mid)
    return (xs[n // 2 - 1], xs[n // 2])


def fw_optimal_cost(sample: Sequence[Num]) -> Num:
    """Sum of nested spreads: the optimal total distance."""
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    return sum((xs[n - 1 - i] - xs[i] for i in range(n // 2)), Fraction(0))


def brute_force_min(sample: Sequence[Num], grid: Iterable[Num]) -> Num:
    """Smallest cost attained on an explicit grid of candidate centres."""
    return min(fw_cost(sample, t) for t in grid)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Median of three, and the clamp (nearest-point projection)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def med3(a: Num, b: Num, c: Num) -> Num:
    """Median of three, in the (max, min) lattice-polynomial form."""
    return max(min(a, b), min(b, c), min(a, c))


def clamp(a: Num, b: Num, x: Num) -> Num:
    """Projection of `x` onto the segment spanned by `a` and `b`."""
    return max(min(a, b), min(max(a, b), x))


def mean3(a: Num, b: Num, x: Num) -> Fraction:
    return Fraction(a + b + x, 1) / 3


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Plane geometry: rays and dilations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cross(p: Tuple[Num, Num], q: Tuple[Num, Num]) -> Num:
    """Twice the signed area of the triangle O, p, q."""
    return p[0] * q[1] - p[1] * q[0]


def on_common_ray(p: Tuple[Num, Num], q: Tuple[Num, Num]) -> bool:
    return cross(p, q) == 0


def triangle_area(p: Tuple[Num, Num], q: Tuple[Num, Num]) -> Fraction:
    return abs(Fraction(cross(p, q))) / 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The measured data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

F = Fraction

KNEES_8X: List[Num] = [F(96), F(112), F(128)]     # ctx = 1024
KNEES_16X: List[Num] = [F(160), F(224), F(256)]   # ctx = 2048
P8, P16 = F(128), F(256)                          # product points d*ctx/32, d = 4

R8 = (F(3, 4), F(7, 8), F(1))                     # normalised 8x triple
R16 = (F(5, 8), F(7, 8), F(1))                    # normalised 16x triple


def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


def check(label: str, ok: bool, detail: str = "") -> None:
    mark = "OK  " if ok else "FAIL"
    print(f"  [{mark}] {label}" + (f"   {detail}" if detail else ""))
    assert ok, label


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 1: the 7/8 median law as a variational statement
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_median_law() -> None:
    rule("1. The 7/8 median law: the centre minimises total distance")

    for name, knees, P in (("8x  (ctx=1024)", KNEES_8X, P8),
                           ("16x (ctx=2048)", KNEES_16X, P16)):
        lo, hi = fermat_weber_set(knees)
        cost = fw_optimal_cost(knees)
        print(f"\n  {name}: knees {[int(k) for k in knees]}, product point P = {int(P)}")
        print(f"    Fermat-Weber set   : [{lo}, {hi}]  (a single point: odd sample)")
        print(f"    optimal cost       : {cost}  (= the spread)")
        print(f"    ratios k*/P        : {[str(k / P) for k in knees]}")
        check("median equals (7/8) * P", lo == F(7, 8) * P, f"{lo} = 7/8 * {int(P)}")
        check("cost at the centre matches the optimum", fw_cost(knees, lo) == cost)
        check("the centre is balanced", is_balanced(knees, lo))

        # strict minimality on a fine grid around the sample
        grid = [F(i, 2) for i in range(int(2 * (min(knees) - 40)), int(2 * (max(knees) + 40)))]
        worse = [t for t in grid if t != lo and fw_cost(knees, t) <= cost]
        check("no other grid point attains the optimum", not worse)
        check("grid minimum equals the theoretical optimum",
              brute_force_min(knees, grid) == cost)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 2: the balance characterisation, all parities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_balance_characterisation() -> None:
    rule("2. Balanced points are exactly the minimisers (any size, any parity)")

    samples: List[List[Num]] = [
        [F(160), F(224), F(256)],
        [F(160), F(224), F(256), F(192)],
        [F(160), F(224), F(256), F(240)],
        [F(5), F(5), F(5), F(9), F(100)],
        [F(0), F(1)],
        [F(7)],
    ]
    for s in samples:
        lo, hi = fermat_weber_set(s)
        grid = [F(i, 2) for i in range(int(2 * (min(s) - 20)), int(2 * (max(s) + 20)) + 1)]
        best = brute_force_min(s, grid)
        minimisers = [t for t in grid if fw_cost(s, t) == best]
        balanced = [t for t in grid if is_balanced(s, t)]
        print(f"\n  sample {[str(x) for x in s]}")
        print(f"    predicted optimal interval : [{lo}, {hi}]")
        print(f"    grid minimisers            : [{min(minimisers)}, {max(minimisers)}]")
        check("minimiser set equals the balanced set", minimisers == balanced)
        check("endpoints match the order-statistic formula",
              (min(minimisers), max(minimisers)) == (lo, hi))
        check("optimal cost equals the nested-spread formula", best == fw_optimal_cost(s))
        # convexity of the minimiser set on the grid
        check("minimiser set is an interval",
              all(fw_cost(s, t) == best for t in grid if lo <= t <= hi))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 3: the median as a projection, and its robustness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_projection() -> None:
    rule("3. The median of three is a nearest-point projection onto a segment")

    a, b = F(224), F(256)   # the two earlier 16x measurements
    print(f"  fixed measurements span the segment [{a}, {b}]")

    xs = [F(i, 2) for i in range(2 * 100, 2 * 400)]
    check("median of three equals the clamp",
          all(med3(a, b, x) == clamp(a, b, x) for x in xs))
    check("the projection lands in the segment",
          all(a <= clamp(a, b, x) <= b for x in xs))
    check("monotone", all(clamp(a, b, xs[i]) <= clamp(a, b, xs[i + 1])
                          for i in range(len(xs) - 1)))
    check("nonexpansive",
          all(abs(clamp(a, b, x) - clamp(a, b, y)) <= abs(x - y)
              for x in xs[::37] for y in xs[::41]))
    check("firmly nonexpansive",
          all((clamp(a, b, x) - clamp(a, b, y)) ** 2
              <= (x - y) * (clamp(a, b, x) - clamp(a, b, y))
              for x in xs[::37] for y in xs[::41]))

    # fibre structure
    stable = [x for x in xs if med3(b, a, x) == F(224)]
    print(f"    values leaving the centre at 224: from {min(stable)} up to {max(stable)}")
    check("the stability fibre is exactly the ray x <= 224",
          all((med3(b, a, x) == F(224)) == (x <= F(224)) for x in xs))
    check("interior fibres are singletons",
          [x for x in xs if clamp(a, b, x) == F(240)] == [F(240)])

    # the measured third value, and the false informal claim
    check("the measured value 160 keeps the centre", med3(b, a, F(160)) == F(224))
    check("its excursion below the segment is 64",
          abs(clamp(a, b, F(160)) - F(160)) == F(64))
    check("every segment point is at least 64 away from 160",
          all(abs(y - F(160)) >= 64 for y in [F(i, 4) for i in range(4 * 224, 4 * 256 + 1)]))
    check("informal claim 'only >= 256 moves the centre' is FALSE",
          med3(b, a, F(240)) == F(240) and F(240) < F(256))

    # contrast with the mean
    m = mean3(b, a, F(160))
    print(f"    mean of the measured triple: {m} = {float(m):.4f}  (not 224)")
    check("the mean is moved off the centre", m != F(224))
    check("the mean is surjective in the free value",
          mean3(b, a, 3 * F(1000) - b - a) == F(1000))
    check("the median's range is the compact segment",
          {med3(a, b, x) for x in xs} == {clamp(a, b, x) for x in xs}
          and min(med3(a, b, x) for x in xs) == a
          and max(med3(a, b, x) for x in xs) == b)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 4: scaling geometry
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_scaling() -> None:
    rule("4. Scaling geometry: two rays, one defect, an exact 3/2 spread ratio")

    top8, top16 = (F(1024), F(128)), (F(2048), F(256))
    med8, med16 = (F(1024), F(112)), (F(2048), F(224))
    low8, low16 = (F(1024), F(96)), (F(2048), F(160))

    check("top edge lies on a ray through the origin", on_common_ray(top8, top16),
          f"slope {top8[1] / top8[0]}")
    check("median lies on a ray through the origin", on_common_ray(med8, med16),
          f"slope {med8[1] / med8[0]} = 7/8 * 1/8")
    check("median slope is 7/8 of the top slope",
          med8[1] / med8[0] == F(7, 8) * (top8[1] / top8[0]))
    check("the slope is forced by one context and confirmed by the other",
          med8[1] / med8[0] == F(7, 64) and F(7, 64) * med16[0] == med16[1])

    check("low tail lies on NO ray", not on_common_ray(low8, low16),
          f"determinant {cross(low8, low16)}, origin triangle area {triangle_area(low8, low16)}")

    check("doubling is equivariant on the top edge", (2 * top8[0], 2 * top8[1]) == top16)
    check("doubling is equivariant on the median", (2 * med8[0], 2 * med8[1]) == med16)
    defect = 2 * low8[1] - low16[1]
    check("low-tail defect equals P/8", defect == F(32) and defect == P16 / 8,
          f"2*96 - 160 = {defect} = {int(P16)}/8")

    factors = {"top": top16[1] / top8[1], "low": low16[1] / low8[1]}
    print(f"    dilation factor forced by the top edge : {factors['top']}")
    print(f"    dilation factor forced by the low tail : {factors['low']}")
    check("no single dilation matches the whole configuration",
          factors["top"] != factors["low"])

    cost8 = fw_optimal_cost(list(R8))
    cost16 = fw_optimal_cost(list(R16))
    print(f"    normalised optimal costs: {cost8} (8x) and {cost16} (16x)")
    check("the 16x spread is exactly 3/2 times the 8x spread",
          cost16 == F(3, 2) * cost8)
    check("the widening is carried entirely by the low coordinate",
          cost16 - cost8 == R8[0] - R16[0] == F(1, 8))
    check("top two normalised coordinates agree at both contexts",
          R8[1:] == R16[1:])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 5: the median level set in R^3
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_level_set() -> None:
    rule("5. A maximal flat face inside a non-convex level set")

    check("both normalised triples have median 7/8",
          med3(*R8) == F(7, 8) and med3(*R16) == F(7, 8))

    edge = [F(i, 32) for i in range(-32, int(32 * F(7, 8)) + 1)]
    check("the whole half-line {(t, 7/8, 1) : t <= 7/8} lies in the level set",
          all(med3(t, F(7, 8), F(1)) == F(7, 8) for t in edge))
    exits = [F(7, 8) + F(i, 64) for i in range(1, 9)]
    check("the edge is maximal: above 7/8 the median moves with t",
          all(med3(t, F(7, 8), F(1)) == t for t in exits))

    for i in range(-8, 17):
        s = F(i, 8)
        pt = tuple(s * u + (1 - s) * v for u, v in zip(R8, R16))
        if s <= 1:
            assert med3(*pt) == F(7, 8)
    check("the segment joining the two contexts stays in the level set "
          "(and extends past it, for all s <= 1)", True)

    u, v = (F(5, 8), F(7, 8), F(1)), (F(7, 8), F(1), F(5, 8))
    mid = tuple((p + q) / 2 for p, q in zip(u, v))
    print(f"    midpoint of two level-set points: {tuple(str(c) for c in mid)}"
          f" has median {med3(*mid)}")
    check("the level set is NOT convex",
          med3(*u) == F(7, 8) and med3(*v) == F(7, 8) and med3(*mid) == F(13, 16))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 6: the pending fourth measurement
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cost16_four(x: Num, t: Num) -> Num:
    return abs(t - 160) + abs(t - 224) + abs(t - 256) + abs(t - x)


def demo_fourth_value() -> None:
    rule("6. The pending fourth measurement: the centre cannot be moved")

    candidates = [F(c) for c in (96, 128, 160, 176, 192, 208, 224, 240, 256, 288, 384)]
    grid = [F(i, 2) for i in range(2 * 50, 2 * 500)]

    print("\n     x    optimal cost    predicted 96+|224-x|    optimal segment")
    for x in candidates:
        best = min(cost16_four(x, t) for t in grid)
        predicted = 96 + abs(224 - x)
        minimisers = [t for t in grid if cost16_four(x, t) == best]
        lo, hi = fermat_weber_set([F(160), F(224), F(256), x])
        print(f"   {int(x):>4}    {str(best):>10}      {str(predicted):>14}"
              f"            [{lo}, {hi}]")
        check(f"224 is optimal for x = {int(x)}",
              all(cost16_four(x, 224) <= cost16_four(x, t) for t in grid))
        check(f"cost law holds for x = {int(x)}", cost16_four(x, F(224)) == predicted)
        check(f"grid optimum matches the law for x = {int(x)}", best == predicted)
        check(f"optimal segment endpoints for x = {int(x)}",
              (min(minimisers), max(minimisers)) == (lo, hi))
        check(f"224 is balanced for x = {int(x)}",
              is_balanced([F(160), F(224), F(256), x], F(224)))
        if F(160) <= x <= F(224):
            check("low regime: the optimal set is [x, 224]", (lo, hi) == (x, F(224)))
        if F(224) <= x <= F(256):
            check("high regime: the optimal set is [224, x]", (lo, hi) == (F(224), x))
        check("uniqueness holds exactly at the knife edge x = 224",
              (lo == hi) == (x == F(224)))


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    demo_median_law()
    demo_balance_characterisation()
    demo_projection()
    demo_scaling()
    demo_level_set()
    demo_fourth_value()
    rule("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Complete Numerical Verification of the Knee-Distribution Geometry
demos.description: A self-contained, exact-rational verification of every quantitative claim in the development. It computes Fermat–Weber costs and minimiser sets for samples of both parities and checks them against the order-statistic formula and against a brute-force grid search; it verifies that the balanced set and the minimiser set coincide exactly, sample by sample; it confirms the 7/8 law median = (7/8)·(d·ctx/32) at both measured contexts together with the optimal costs 96 and 32; it audits the clamp/projection identity for the median of three, including monotonicity, nonexpansiveness, firm nonexpansiveness, the half-line stability fibre, and the refutation of the informal threshold 256 by the value 240; it checks the plane-geometry claims (ray determinants, the origin-triangle area 16384, dilation equivariance and the low-tail defect 32 = P/8, and the exact 3/2 spread ratio); it verifies the maximal flat edge of the median level set in R^3 and its non-convexity; and it tabulates the full fourth-measurement prediction, confirming for eleven candidate values that 224 stays optimal, that the cost equals 96 + |224 − x|, and that the optimal segment endpoints follow the two regime formulas.
demos.code:
"""
Numerical demonstration of the geometry of a knee distribution.

This script is fully self-contained (standard library only, exact rational
arithmetic where it matters) and verifies, numerically, every quantitative
claim of the accompanying article and paper:

  1. Fermat-Weber cost on a line, its minimiser set, and the balance
     characterisation of optimality (any sample size, either parity).
  2. The measured three-value knee distributions at two context lengths, their
     geometric medians, and the 7/8 law  median = (7/8) * (d*ctx/32).
  3. The median of three as a nearest-point projection (clamp): monotonicity,
     nonexpansiveness, firm nonexpansiveness, fibre structure, range;
     the refutation of the informal claim "only values >= 256 move the centre".
  4. Scaling geometry: rays through the origin, the doubling dilation, the
     low-tail defect P/8, and the exact 3/2 spread ratio.
  5. The median level set in R^3: a maximal flat edge, the segment joining the
     two normalised measurements, and non-convexity of the level set.
  6. The pre-registered prediction for a pending fourth measurement: the centre
     224 stays optimal for every fourth value, the cost law 96 + |224 - x|,
     the two regimes, and the uniqueness knife edge.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Num = Fraction


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Fermat-Weber cost, minimiser set, and the balance certificate
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def fw_cost(sample: Sequence[Num], t: Num) -> Num:
    """Total distance from the candidate centre `t` to every sample point."""
    return sum((abs(t - x) for x in sample), Fraction(0))


def is_balanced(sample: Sequence[Num], m: Num) -> bool:
    """`m` is balanced: neither open side of `m` holds more than half the sample."""
    n_le = sum(1 for x in sample if x <= m)
    n_lt = sum(1 for x in sample if x < m)
    n = len(sample)
    return (n - n_le) <= n_le and n_lt <= (n - n_lt)


def fermat_weber_set(sample: Sequence[Num]) -> Tuple[Num, Num]:
    """Endpoints of the interval of minimisers of the total distance.

    Odd size 2k+1: the singleton [x_(k+1), x_(k+1)].
    Even size 2k : the middle segment [x_(k), x_(k+1)].
    """
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    if n % 2 == 1:
        mid = xs[n // 2]
        return (mid, mid)
    return (xs[n // 2 - 1], xs[n // 2])


def fw_optimal_cost(sample: Sequence[Num]) -> Num:
    """Sum of nested spreads: the optimal total distance."""
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    return sum((xs[n - 1 - i] - xs[i] for i in range(n // 2)), Fraction(0))


def brute_force_min(sample: Sequence[Num], grid: Iterable[Num]) -> Num:
    """Smallest cost attained on an explicit grid of candidate centres."""
    return min(fw_cost(sample, t) for t in grid)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Median of three, and the clamp (nearest-point projection)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def med3(a: Num, b: Num, c: Num) -> Num:
    """Median of three, in the (max, min) lattice-polynomial form."""
    return max(min(a, b), min(b, c), min(a, c))


def clamp(a: Num, b: Num, x: Num) -> Num:
    """Projection of `x` onto the segment spanned by `a` and `b`."""
    return max(min(a, b), min(max(a, b), x))


def mean3(a: Num, b: Num, x: Num) -> Fraction:
    return Fraction(a + b + x, 1) / 3


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Plane geometry: rays and dilations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cross(p: Tuple[Num, Num], q: Tuple[Num, Num]) -> Num:
    """Twice the signed area of the triangle O, p, q."""
    return p[0] * q[1] - p[1] * q[0]


def on_common_ray(p: Tuple[Num, Num], q: Tuple[Num, Num]) -> bool:
    return cross(p, q) == 0


def triangle_area(p: Tuple[Num, Num], q: Tuple[Num, Num]) -> Fraction:
    return abs(Fraction(cross(p, q))) / 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The measured data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

F = Fraction

KNEES_8X: List[Num] = [F(96), F(112), F(128)]     # ctx = 1024
KNEES_16X: List[Num] = [F(160), F(224), F(256)]   # ctx = 2048
P8, P16 = F(128), F(256)                          # product points d*ctx/32, d = 4

R8 = (F(3, 4), F(7, 8), F(1))                     # normalised 8x triple
R16 = (F(5, 8), F(7, 8), F(1))                    # normalised 16x triple


def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


def check(label: str, ok: bool, detail: str = "") -> None:
    mark = "OK  " if ok else "FAIL"
    print(f"  [{mark}] {label}" + (f"   {detail}" if detail else ""))
    assert ok, label


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 1: the 7/8 median law as a variational statement
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_median_law() -> None:
    rule("1. The 7/8 median law: the centre minimises total distance")

    for name, knees, P in (("8x  (ctx=1024)", KNEES_8X, P8),
                           ("16x (ctx=2048)", KNEES_16X, P16)):
        lo, hi = fermat_weber_set(knees)
        cost = fw_optimal_cost(knees)
        print(f"\n  {name}: knees {[int(k) for k in knees]}, product point P = {int(P)}")
        print(f"    Fermat-Weber set   : [{lo}, {hi}]  (a single point: odd sample)")
        print(f"    optimal cost       : {cost}  (= the spread)")
        print(f"    ratios k*/P        : {[str(k / P) for k in knees]}")
        check("median equals (7/8) * P", lo == F(7, 8) * P, f"{lo} = 7/8 * {int(P)}")
        check("cost at the centre matches the optimum", fw_cost(knees, lo) == cost)
        check("the centre is balanced", is_balanced(knees, lo))

        # strict minimality on a fine grid around the sample
        grid = [F(i, 2) for i in range(int(2 * (min(knees) - 40)), int(2 * (max(knees) + 40)))]
        worse = [t for t in grid if t != lo and fw_cost(knees, t) <= cost]
        check("no other grid point attains the optimum", not worse)
        check("grid minimum equals the theoretical optimum",
              brute_force_min(knees, grid) == cost)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 2: the balance characterisation, all parities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_balance_characterisation() -> None:
    rule("2. Balanced points are exactly the minimisers (any size, any parity)")

    samples: List[List[Num]] = [
        [F(160), F(224), F(256)],
        [F(160), F(224), F(256), F(192)],
        [F(160), F(224), F(256), F(240)],
        [F(5), F(5), F(5), F(9), F(100)],
        [F(0), F(1)],
        [F(7)],
    ]
    for s in samples:
        lo, hi = fermat_weber_set(s)
        grid = [F(i, 2) for i in range(int(2 * (min(s) - 20)), int(2 * (max(s) + 20)) + 1)]
        best = brute_force_min(s, grid)
        minimisers = [t for t in grid if fw_cost(s, t) == best]
        balanced = [t for t in grid if is_balanced(s, t)]
        print(f"\n  sample {[str(x) for x in s]}")
        print(f"    predicted optimal interval : [{lo}, {hi}]")
        print(f"    grid minimisers            : [{min(minimisers)}, {max(minimisers)}]")
        check("minimiser set equals the balanced set", minimisers == balanced)
        check("endpoints match the order-statistic formula",
              (min(minimisers), max(minimisers)) == (lo, hi))
        check("optimal cost equals the nested-spread formula", best == fw_optimal_cost(s))
        # convexity of the minimiser set on the grid
        check("minimiser set is an interval",
              all(fw_cost(s, t) == best for t in grid if lo <= t <= hi))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 3: the median as a projection, and its robustness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_projection() -> None:
    rule("3. The median of three is a nearest-point projection onto a segment")

    a, b = F(224), F(256)   # the two earlier 16x measurements
    print(f"  fixed measurements span the segment [{a}, {b}]")

    xs = [F(i, 2) for i in range(2 * 100, 2 * 400)]
    check("median of three equals the clamp",
          all(med3(a, b, x) == clamp(a, b, x) for x in xs))
    check("the projection lands in the segment",
          all(a <= clamp(a, b, x) <= b for x in xs))
    check("monotone", all(clamp(a, b, xs[i]) <= clamp(a, b, xs[i + 1])
                          for i in range(len(xs) - 1)))
    check("nonexpansive",
          all(abs(clamp(a, b, x) - clamp(a, b, y)) <= abs(x - y)
              for x in xs[::37] for y in xs[::41]))
    check("firmly nonexpansive",
          all((clamp(a, b, x) - clamp(a, b, y)) ** 2
              <= (x - y) * (clamp(a, b, x) - clamp(a, b, y))
              for x in xs[::37] for y in xs[::41]))

    # fibre structure
    stable = [x for x in xs if med3(b, a, x) == F(224)]
    print(f"    values leaving the centre at 224: from {min(stable)} up to {max(stable)}")
    check("the stability fibre is exactly the ray x <= 224",
          all((med3(b, a, x) == F(224)) == (x <= F(224)) for x in xs))
    check("interior fibres are singletons",
          [x for x in xs if clamp(a, b, x) == F(240)] == [F(240)])

    # the measured third value, and the false informal claim
    check("the measured value 160 keeps the centre", med3(b, a, F(160)) == F(224))
    check("its excursion below the segment is 64",
          abs(clamp(a, b, F(160)) - F(160)) == F(64))
    check("every segment point is at least 64 away from 160",
          all(abs(y - F(160)) >= 64 for y in [F(i, 4) for i in range(4 * 224, 4 * 256 + 1)]))
    check("informal claim 'only >= 256 moves the centre' is FALSE",
          med3(b, a, F(240)) == F(240) and F(240) < F(256))

    # contrast with the mean
    m = mean3(b, a, F(160))
    print(f"    mean of the measured triple: {m} = {float(m):.4f}  (not 224)")
    check("the mean is moved off the centre", m != F(224))
    check("the mean is surjective in the free value",
          mean3(b, a, 3 * F(1000) - b - a) == F(1000))
    check("the median's range is the compact segment",
          {med3(a, b, x) for x in xs} == {clamp(a, b, x) for x in xs}
          and min(med3(a, b, x) for x in xs) == a
          and max(med3(a, b, x) for x in xs) == b)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 4: scaling geometry
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_scaling() -> None:
    rule("4. Scaling geometry: two rays, one defect, an exact 3/2 spread ratio")

    top8, top16 = (F(1024), F(128)), (F(2048), F(256))
    med8, med16 = (F(1024), F(112)), (F(2048), F(224))
    low8, low16 = (F(1024), F(96)), (F(2048), F(160))

    check("top edge lies on a ray through the origin", on_common_ray(top8, top16),
          f"slope {top8[1] / top8[0]}")
    check("median lies on a ray through the origin", on_common_ray(med8, med16),
          f"slope {med8[1] / med8[0]} = 7/8 * 1/8")
    check("median slope is 7/8 of the top slope",
          med8[1] / med8[0] == F(7, 8) * (top8[1] / top8[0]))
    check("the slope is forced by one context and confirmed by the other",
          med8[1] / med8[0] == F(7, 64) and F(7, 64) * med16[0] == med16[1])

    check("low tail lies on NO ray", not on_common_ray(low8, low16),
          f"determinant {cross(low8, low16)}, origin triangle area {triangle_area(low8, low16)}")

    check("doubling is equivariant on the top edge", (2 * top8[0], 2 * top8[1]) == top16)
    check("doubling is equivariant on the median", (2 * med8[0], 2 * med8[1]) == med16)
    defect = 2 * low8[1] - low16[1]
    check("low-tail defect equals P/8", defect == F(32) and defect == P16 / 8,
          f"2*96 - 160 = {defect} = {int(P16)}/8")

    factors = {"top": top16[1] / top8[1], "low": low16[1] / low8[1]}
    print(f"    dilation factor forced by the top edge : {factors['top']}")
    print(f"    dilation factor forced by the low tail : {factors['low']}")
    check("no single dilation matches the whole configuration",
          factors["top"] != factors["low"])

    cost8 = fw_optimal_cost(list(R8))
    cost16 = fw_optimal_cost(list(R16))
    print(f"    normalised optimal costs: {cost8} (8x) and {cost16} (16x)")
    check("the 16x spread is exactly 3/2 times the 8x spread",
          cost16 == F(3, 2) * cost8)
    check("the widening is carried entirely by the low coordinate",
          cost16 - cost8 == R8[0] - R16[0] == F(1, 8))
    check("top two normalised coordinates agree at both contexts",
          R8[1:] == R16[1:])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 5: the median level set in R^3
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_level_set() -> None:
    rule("5. A maximal flat face inside a non-convex level set")

    check("both normalised triples have median 7/8",
          med3(*R8) == F(7, 8) and med3(*R16) == F(7, 8))

    edge = [F(i, 32) for i in range(-32, int(32 * F(7, 8)) + 1)]
    check("the whole half-line {(t, 7/8, 1) : t <= 7/8} lies in the level set",
          all(med3(t, F(7, 8), F(1)) == F(7, 8) for t in edge))
    exits = [F(7, 8) + F(i, 64) for i in range(1, 9)]
    check("the edge is maximal: above 7/8 the median moves with t",
          all(med3(t, F(7, 8), F(1)) == t for t in exits))

    for i in range(-8, 17):
        s = F(i, 8)
        pt = tuple(s * u + (1 - s) * v for u, v in zip(R8, R16))
        if s <= 1:
            assert med3(*pt) == F(7, 8)
    check("the segment joining the two contexts stays in the level set "
          "(and extends past it, for all s <= 1)", True)

    u, v = (F(5, 8), F(7, 8), F(1)), (F(7, 8), F(1), F(5, 8))
    mid = tuple((p + q) / 2 for p, q in zip(u, v))
    print(f"    midpoint of two level-set points: {tuple(str(c) for c in mid)}"
          f" has median {med3(*mid)}")
    check("the level set is NOT convex",
          med3(*u) == F(7, 8) and med3(*v) == F(7, 8) and med3(*mid) == F(13, 16))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 6: the pending fourth measurement
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cost16_four(x: Num, t: Num) -> Num:
    return abs(t - 160) + abs(t - 224) + abs(t - 256) + abs(t - x)


def demo_fourth_value() -> None:
    rule("6. The pending fourth measurement: the centre cannot be moved")

    candidates = [F(c) for c in (96, 128, 160, 176, 192, 208, 224, 240, 256, 288, 384)]
    grid = [F(i, 2) for i in range(2 * 50, 2 * 500)]

    print("\n     x    optimal cost    predicted 96+|224-x|    optimal segment")
    for x in candidates:
        best = min(cost16_four(x, t) for t in grid)
        predicted = 96 + abs(224 - x)
        minimisers = [t for t in grid if cost16_four(x, t) == best]
        lo, hi = fermat_weber_set([F(160), F(224), F(256), x])
        print(f"   {int(x):>4}    {str(best):>10}      {str(predicted):>14}"
              f"            [{lo}, {hi}]")
        check(f"224 is optimal for x = {int(x)}",
              all(cost16_four(x, 224) <= cost16_four(x, t) for t in grid))
        check(f"cost law holds for x = {int(x)}", cost16_four(x, F(224)) == predicted)
        check(f"grid optimum matches the law for x = {int(x)}", best == predicted)
        check(f"optimal segment endpoints for x = {int(x)}",
              (min(minimisers), max(minimisers)) == (lo, hi))
        check(f"224 is balanced for x = {int(x)}",
              is_balanced([F(160), F(224), F(256), x], F(224)))
        if F(160) <= x <= F(224):
            check("low regime: the optimal set is [x, 224]", (lo, hi) == (x, F(224)))
        if F(224) <= x <= F(256):
            check("high regime: the optimal set is [224, x]", (lo, hi) == (F(224), x))
        check("uniqueness holds exactly at the knife edge x = 224",
              (lo == hi) == (x == F(224)))


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    demo_median_law()
    demo_balance_characterisation()
    demo_projection()
    demo_scaling()
    demo_level_set()
    demo_fourth_value()
    rule("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Robustness Audit: The Stability Half-Line of a Reported Centre
demos.description: A focused audit of why the reported centre survives a wild measurement. Holding two measurements fixed at 224 and 256, it sweeps the free measurement across a wide range and tabulates the reported median beside the arithmetic mean, exhibiting the moment the centre finally moves; it then computes the exact stability set of the reported centre — the half-line (−∞, 224], the normal cone of the segment at its lower endpoint — and shows the measured value 160 lies inside it with unbounded room, while 240, below the naively assumed threshold of 256, already moves the centre. It verifies monotonicity, nonexpansiveness and firm nonexpansiveness of the projection in exact arithmetic, contrasts the median's compact range [224, 256] with the mean's unbounded affine response, and quantifies the absorbed excursion as exactly 64 units.

algorithms.name: Exact Fermat–Weber Set via Order Statistics
algorithms.description: Computes the full set of minimisers of the total-distance functional F(t) = Σ|t − x| for a one-dimensional sample, together with the optimal cost, without any numerical optimisation. The mathematical foundation is the piecewise-linear structure of F: its slope at t is #{x < t} − #{x > t}, so the minimiser set is precisely the stretch on which the two counts agree. For odd size 2k+1 this is the single counting median x_(k+1); for even size 2k it is the middle segment [x_(k), x_(k+1)], which degenerates to a point exactly when the two middle order statistics coincide. The optimal cost is the sum of nested spreads Σ (x_(n−i) − x_(i+1)) over i < ⌊n/2⌋, i.e. the diameter for three points and (d − a) + (c − b) for four. Complexity is O(n log n) as written (dominated by the sort) and O(n) if a linear-time selection routine is substituted; space is O(n). This is the entry point of the pipeline: every downstream statement — the 7/8 law, the spread ratio, the fourth-measurement regimes — is a reading of the interval this routine returns.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  : a finite multiset S = {x_1, ..., x_n} of reals, n >= 1
OUTPUT : the closed interval [lo, hi] of minimisers of F(t) = sum |t - x_i|,
         and the optimal value F(lo)

1.  x <- SORT(S)                            // or two selections, O(n)
2.  n <- |x|
3.  if n is odd then
4.      m   <- x[(n+1)/2]                   // the counting median
5.      lo, hi <- m, m                      // minimiser is unique
6.  else
7.      lo  <- x[n/2]                       // lower middle order statistic
8.      hi  <- x[n/2 + 1]                   // upper middle order statistic
9.  end if
10. cost <- 0
11. for i <- 1 to floor(n/2) do
12.     cost <- cost + (x[n + 1 - i] - x[i])   // nested spreads
13. end for
14. return ([lo, hi], cost)

CORRECTNESS: F is convex and piecewise linear with slope
  #{x < t} - #{x > t}; the slope is <= 0 left of lo and >= 0 right of hi,
  and identically 0 on [lo, hi]. Equivalently, [lo, hi] is exactly the set
  of balanced points.

algorithms.name: Balance Certificate for ℓ¹ Optimality
algorithms.description: Decides, in a single pass and using only order comparisons, whether a proposed centre minimises the total distance to a sample — and, when it does not, exhibits an explicit improving witness. The foundation is the characterisation theorem: m is optimal if and only if it is balanced, meaning #{x > m} ≤ #{x ≤ m} and #{x < m} ≤ #{x ≥ m}. Sufficiency is a counting argument valid in any linearly ordered abelian group: stepping from m by δ makes each near-side datum pay δ and each far-side datum refund at most δ, and balance says the payers are at least as numerous. Necessity is finitary: if one side is strictly heavier, the step to the nearest datum on that side jumps over no data, so the cost changes exactly linearly by (light − heavy)·δ < 0. Complexity is O(n) time and O(1) space, strictly cheaper than evaluating the objective, and the test never performs arithmetic on the data values — a useful property for exact or symbolic inputs. In the pipeline it serves as the optimality proof attached to any reported centre, including the four-measurement claim that 224 stays optimal for every possible fourth value.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  : a finite multiset S, a candidate centre m
OUTPUT : TRUE with an optimality certificate, or FALSE with an improving
         witness t satisfying F(t) < F(m)

1.  lt, eq, gt <- 0, 0, 0
2.  for each x in S do                       // single pass, comparisons only
3.      if   x < m then lt <- lt + 1
4.      elif x > m then gt <- gt + 1
5.      else            eq <- eq + 1
6.  end for
7.  balanced <- (gt <= lt + eq) and (lt <= gt + eq)
8.  if balanced then
9.      return (TRUE, certificate = (lt, eq, gt))
10. end if
11. if gt > lt + eq then                     // heavy above
12.     t <- min { x in S : x > m }          // nearest datum above
13. else                                     // heavy below
14.     t <- max { x in S : x < m }          // nearest datum below
15. end if
16. return (FALSE, witness = t)

GUARANTEE: the step m -> t crosses no datum, so
  F(t) = F(m) + (#{x <= m} - #{x > m}) * (t - m)  exactly,
  which is strictly negative in the unbalanced case.
algorithms.code:
"""Balance certificate: an O(n) exact optimality test for the geometric median."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Sequence, Tuple


def balance_counts(sample: Sequence[float], m: float) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Return (#{x < m}, #{x == m}, #{x > m}) in a single pass. O(n)."""
    lt = eq = gt = 0
    for x in sample:
        if x < m:
            lt += 1
        elif x > m:
            gt += 1
        else:
            eq += 1
    return lt, eq, gt


def is_balanced(sample: Sequence[float], m: float) -> bool:
    """True iff neither open side of m holds more than half the sample.

    Formally: #{x > m} <= #{x <= m} and #{x < m} <= #{x >= m}.  By the
    characterisation theorem this holds exactly when m minimises the total
    distance, so the predicate is a complete optimality certificate that
    performs no arithmetic on the data values beyond comparisons. O(n) time,
    O(1) space.
    """
    lt, eq, gt = balance_counts(sample, m)
    return gt <= lt + eq and lt <= gt + eq


def certify(sample: Sequence[float], m: float) -> str:
    """Human-readable certificate, including the direction of improvement."""
    lt, eq, gt = balance_counts(sample, m)
    if is_balanced(sample, m):
        return (f"m = {m} is balanced ({lt} below, {eq} at, {gt} above) "
                f"=> m minimises the total distance")
    heavy = "above" if gt > lt + eq else "below"
    witness = (min((x for x in sample if x > m), default=None) if heavy == "above"
               else max((x for x in sample if x < m), default=None))
    return (f"m = {m} is unbalanced ({lt} below, {eq} at, {gt} above): the {heavy} "
            f"side is strictly heavier, and stepping to the nearest datum {witness} "
            f"strictly decreases the cost")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = [160.0, 224.0, 256.0, 192.0]
    for m in (160.0, 192.0, 208.0, 224.0, 240.0):
        print(certify(data, m))

algorithms.name: Stability Radius of a Reported Centre Under One Free Measurement
algorithms.description: Given two fixed measurements and one free one, returns the exact set of values of the free measurement that leave a reported centre unchanged, together with the downward and upward slack. The foundation is the projection identity med(a, b, x) = max(a ∧ b, min(a ∨ b, x)): as a function of the free coordinate the median is the nearest-point projection onto the segment spanned by the fixed pair. Fibres of a projection over the endpoints are closed half-lines — the normal cones of the segment there — and over interior points are singletons, so a centre reported at an endpoint enjoys unbounded stability in one direction while an interior centre has none at all. Complexity is O(1) after reading the fixed pair (O(n) in general, from the two middle order statistics). In the pipeline this is the quantitative statement of robustness: for the measured data the stability set is the half-line (−∞, 224], which contains the measured value 160 with infinite room and simultaneously refutes the informal threshold of 256, since 240 already lies outside it.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  : two fixed measurements a, b; a reported centre m
OUTPUT : the interval of free values x with med(a, b, x) = m,
         plus the downward and upward slack

1.  lo, hi <- min(a, b), max(a, b)          // the fixed segment
2.  if m < lo or m > hi then
3.      return (EMPTY, 'unreachable: m lies off the segment')
4.  end if
5.  if lo = hi then
6.      return ((-inf, +inf), 'degenerate segment: every x works')
7.  end if
8.  if m = lo then
9.      return ((-inf, lo], slack_down = +inf, slack_up = 0)
10. elif m = hi then
11.     return ([hi, +inf), slack_down = 0, slack_up = +inf)
12. else
13.     return ({m}, slack_down = 0, slack_up = 0)
14. end if

READING: unbounded slack occurs exactly when the reported centre sits at an
  endpoint of the segment spanned by the fixed data; this is the boundary
  phenomenon responsible for the observed robustness.

algorithms.name: Ray and Dilation Diagnostics for Two-Point Scaling Laws
algorithms.description: Tests whether two measurements taken at different scales obey a common proportional law, quantifies the departure when they do not, and measures the failure of equivariance under a doubling dilation. The foundation is elementary plane geometry: two points p, q lie on a common ray through the origin exactly when the 2×2 determinant p₁q₂ − p₂q₁ vanishes, and half its absolute value is the area of the triangle O, p, q, giving a scale-aware measure of non-proportionality. When the determinant vanishes the common slope is the unique constant of the fitted law, so a law fitted on one scale is genuinely tested — not refitted — on the next. For a doubling pair the scalar 2p₂ − q₂ is the dilation defect. Complexity is O(1) per pair, in exact rational arithmetic. Applied to the measurement families this yields: top edge on a ray of slope 1/8, median on a ray of slope 7/64 = (7/8)(1/8), low tail on no ray with determinant −32768 and origin triangle area 16384, and low-tail dilation defect exactly 32 = P/8 — the single scalar in which all the non-self-similarity of the distribution is concentrated.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  : paired measurements p = (c1, y1) and q = (c2, y2), c2 = 2 * c1
OUTPUT : ray verdict, fitted slope or triangle area, dilation defect,
         and a fit-then-test report

1.  det <- c1 * y2 - y1 * c2                       // exact rational
2.  if det = 0 then
3.      slope <- y1 / c1
4.      verdict <- ('proportional law', slope)
5.  else
6.      area <- |det| / 2                          // origin triangle
7.      verdict <- ('no proportional law', area)
8.  end if
9.  defect <- 2 * y1 - y2                          // dilation equivariance
10. // fit on the short scale, test on the long one
11. s <- y1 / c1
12. predicted <- s * c2
13. report <- (predicted = y2) ? 'confirmed' : 'refuted'
14. return (verdict, defect, predicted, report)

NOTE: step 11 has no free parameter — one measurement determines s — so
  step 13 is a genuine out-of-sample test rather than a second fit.
algorithms.code:
"""Ray and dilation diagnostics for two-point scaling laws."""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, Sequence, Tuple

Point = Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]


def cross(p: Point, q: Point) -> Fraction:
    """Twice the signed area of the triangle with vertices O, p, q. O(1)."""
    return p[0] * q[1] - p[1] * q[0]


def ray_diagnostic(p: Point, q: Point) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Test whether two measurements obey a common proportional law.

    Two plane points lie on a common ray through the origin exactly when the
    2x2 determinant vanishes; the magnitude of the determinant, halved, is the
    area of the origin triangle and quantifies departure from proportionality.
    When the points are proportional the common slope is returned, which is the
    unique constant of the fitted law. O(1) exact rational arithmetic.
    """
    det = cross(p, q)
    out: Dict[str, object] = {
        "determinant": det,
        "on_common_ray": det == 0,
        "origin_triangle_area": abs(det) / 2,
    }
    if det == 0 and p[0] != 0:
        out["slope"] = p[1] / p[0]
    return out


def dilation_defect(p: Point, q: Point, factor: Fraction = Fraction(2)) -> Fraction:
    """Failure of equivariance under the dilation by `factor`.

    If q is the measurement at `factor` times the abscissa of p, the defect is
    factor * p_y - q_y: zero exactly when the dilation carries p to q. O(1).
    """
    return factor * p[1] - q[1]


def fit_and_test(short: Point, long_: Point) -> str:
    """Fit a proportional law on the short-context point and test it on the long one."""
    slope = short[1] / short[0]
    predicted = slope * long_[0]
    verdict = "confirmed" if predicted == long_[1] else "refuted"
    return (f"slope forced by {short} is {slope}; it predicts {predicted} at "
            f"abscissa {long_[0]}, measured {long_[1]} -> {verdict}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    F = Fraction
    families: Sequence[Tuple[str, Point, Point]] = [
        ("top edge", (F(1024), F(128)), (F(2048), F(256))),
        ("median", (F(1024), F(112)), (F(2048), F(224))),
        ("low tail", (F(1024), F(96)), (F(2048), F(160))),
    ]
    for name, p, q in families:
        d = ray_diagnostic(p, q)
        print(f"{name:>9}: {d}")
        print(f"{'':>9}  dilation defect {dilation_defect(p, q)}")
        print(f"{'':>9}  {fit_and_test(p, q)}")

visualizations.name: Cost Landscapes: From a Unique Centre to an Optimal Segment
visualizations.description: Four panels of the total-distance functional F(t) = Σ|t − x| over a common range of candidate centres: the measured three-value distribution {160, 224, 256}, whose landscape has a single sharp corner at the 7/8 centre 224, and the same data extended by a hypothetical fourth value at 192 (low tail repeats), 240 (high) and 224 (the knife edge). Each panel shades the optimal set, marks the 7/8 centre with a reference line, and plots the measurements themselves, making visible that the flat bottom appears exactly when the sample size is even and that 224 is always one of its endpoints.
visualizations.code:
"""Cost landscapes: odd samples give a point, even samples give a segment.

Plots the total-distance functional F(t) = sum |t - x_i| for the measured
three-value knee distribution {160, 224, 256} and for the same data extended by
a hypothetical fourth value, showing that the minimiser degenerates from a
single point (the 7/8 centre 224) into a segment with 224 always an endpoint.

Requires: matplotlib, numpy.  Writes cost_landscapes.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def fw_cost(sample: Sequence[float], t: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    return sum(np.abs(t - x) for x in sample)


def fw_set(sample: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    if n % 2 == 1:
        return xs[n // 2], xs[n // 2]
    return xs[n // 2 - 1], xs[n // 2]


def main() -> None:
    grid = np.linspace(120.0, 300.0, 2001)
    base: List[float] = [160.0, 224.0, 256.0]
    panels: List[Tuple[str, List[float]]] = [
        ("three measurements {160, 224, 256}: unique centre 224", base),
        ("fourth value 192 (low tail repeats): optimum [192, 224]", base + [192.0]),
        ("fourth value 240 (high): optimum [224, 240]", base + [240.0]),
        ("fourth value 224 (knife edge): optimum still unique", base + [224.0]),
    ]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12.5, 8.0), sharex=True)
    for ax, (title, sample) in zip(axes.ravel(), panels):
        ax.plot(grid, fw_cost(sample, grid), lw=2.0, color="#1f77b4")
        lo, hi = fw_set(sample)
        opt = float(fw_cost(sample, np.array([lo]))[0])
        ax.axvspan(lo, hi if hi > lo else lo + 0.6, color="#1f77b4", alpha=0.18,
                   label=f"optimal set [{lo:g}, {hi:g}]")
        ax.axvline(224, color="#2ca02c", ls="--", lw=1.3, label="224 = (7/8)·256")
        ax.scatter(sample, [opt * 0.985] * len(sample), color="#d62728", zorder=5,
                   s=34, label="measurements")
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
        ax.set_ylabel("total distance  F(t)")
        ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
        ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper center")
    for ax in axes[1]:
        ax.set_xlabel("candidate centre  t")

    fig.suptitle("Fermat–Weber landscapes: the centre 224 is always optimal, "
                 "and always an endpoint of the optimal set", fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("cost_landscapes.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote cost_landscapes.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Scaling Rays: Two Proportional Laws and One Defect
visualizations.description: The six measurements plotted as points (ctx, k*) in the plane, with the ray through the origin of slope 1/8 fitted by the top edge, the ray of slope 7/64 = (7/8)(1/8) fitted by the median, and the ray of slope 3/32 that the short-context low tail would demand. The plot shows that the first two rays pass exactly through both of their measurements while the third overshoots at the long context: the doubling dilation sends the short-context low tail to 192 while the measured value is 160, an annotated defect of exactly 32 = P/8. It is the picture behind the statement that the centre and the upper edge are dilation-equivariant while the distribution as a whole is not self-similar.
visualizations.code:
"""Scaling rays: two proportional laws and one defect.

Plots the six measurements as points (ctx, k*) in the plane, draws the rays
through the origin fitted by the top edge (slope 1/8) and by the median
(slope 7/64 = (7/8)(1/8)), and shows that the low tail lies on no ray: the
doubling dilation sends (1024, 96) to (2048, 192) while the measured value is
(2048, 160), a defect of exactly 32 = P/8.

Requires: matplotlib, numpy.  Writes scaling_rays.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def main() -> None:
    ctxs = np.array([1024.0, 2048.0])
    top = np.array([128.0, 256.0])
    med = np.array([112.0, 224.0])
    low = np.array([96.0, 160.0])

    line = np.linspace(0.0, 2300.0, 200)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 6.4))

    ax.plot(line, line / 8.0, color="#1f77b4", lw=1.6, alpha=0.85,
            label="top-edge ray, slope 1/8  (product point $P=d\\,\\mathrm{ctx}/32$)")
    ax.plot(line, line * 7.0 / 64.0, color="#2ca02c", lw=1.6, alpha=0.85,
            label="median ray, slope 7/64 = (7/8)(1/8)")
    ax.plot(line, line * 96.0 / 1024.0, color="#d62728", lw=1.2, ls=":", alpha=0.8,
            label="ray fitted to the short-context low tail (slope 3/32)")

    ax.scatter(ctxs, top, s=70, color="#1f77b4", zorder=5, label="top measurements")
    ax.scatter(ctxs, med, s=70, color="#2ca02c", zorder=5, label="median")
    ax.scatter(ctxs, low, s=70, color="#d62728", zorder=5, label="low tail")

    ax.scatter([2048.0], [192.0], s=90, facecolors="none", edgecolors="#d62728",
               lw=1.8, zorder=5, label="doubled low tail (predicted 192)")
    ax.annotate("", xy=(2048, 160), xytext=(2048, 192),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#d62728", lw=1.6))
    ax.text(2075, 174, "defect 32 = P/8", color="#d62728", fontsize=10)

    for c, y, txt in [(1024, 128, "128"), (2048, 256, "256"),
                      (1024, 112, "112"), (2048, 224, "224"),
                      (1024, 96, "96"), (2048, 160, "160")]:
        ax.annotate(txt, (c, y), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-26, -4), fontsize=9)

    ax.set_xlim(0, 2400)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 320)
    ax.set_xlabel("context length  ctx")
    ax.set_ylabel("knee  $k^{*}$")
    ax.set_title("The top edge and the median are rays through the origin; the low tail is not")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
    ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("scaling_rays.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote scaling_rays.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Fermat–Weber Laboratory: Drag the Data, Watch the Centre Refuse to Move
interactive_demos.description: A single, deeply-built widget in which the reader manipulates the measurements directly and reads the geometry off the curve. It plots the total-distance functional F(t) = Σ|t − x| live as four sliders move the measurements, shades the exact set of minimising centres, and marks the 7/8 centre 224 with a reference line. Toggling the fourth measurement on and off flips the sample's parity and makes the optimum switch between a single point and a segment; whatever the fourth slider is set to, one endpoint of the shaded band stays locked at 224, and a live readout compares the measured optimal cost against the predicted law 96 + |224 − x|. A second toggle overlays the arithmetic mean, which visibly chases every wild measurement while the median does not. Beneath the plot, a balance table recomputes the counting certificate #{x < t}, #{x = t}, #{x > t} at several candidate centres and reports 'balanced ⇒ optimal' or 'unbalanced ⇒ not optimal' in real time, so the reader can watch the characterisation theorem decide optimality by counting alone. Three collapsible sections supply the proofs — the middle-segment equality criterion, the balance certificate with its finitary improving witness, and the two-triangle-inequality argument that pins 224 for every possible fourth value.
interactive_demos.html:
The Fermat–Weber Laboratory

Drag the measurements. The curve is the total distance F(t) = Σ |t − xi|; the shaded band is the set of centres that minimise it. Watch two things: with an odd number of measurements the optimum is a single point, and with an even number it is a whole segment — and no matter where you drag the fourth measurement, the value 224 stays on the boundary of that segment.

—
